e.etymology: An African-American name of the 1970s made by adding the La- prefix to Kesha, a spelling of Keisha.
An American name of the early 1900s that crosses Bernice with the Vern- of Vernon and Verna.
An American name of around 1900 that sits beside Verna and Vera. It is often linked with the Latin root for green, as in verdant.
A shortened spelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques. Jacques is the French form of James and Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov, traditionally supplanter.
A pet form of Geraldine, the feminine of Gerald, from the Germanic elements ger (spear) and wald (rule).
namesakes: Geri Halliwell (Ginger Spice of the Spice Girls)

e.etymology: A spelling of Lori, a pet form of Laura and Lorraine. Laura comes from Latin laurus, the laurel tree whose leaves crowned victors.
An American name of the 1970s close in sound to Shonda, Shawna and Sandra.
e.note: In Yiddish a shanda is a shame or a scandal.

e.etymology: A variant of Orville, a name Fanny Burney created for Lord Orville, the hero of her 1778 novel Evelina, perhaps with French or and ville, gold and town, in mind.
A spelling of Doreen, formed in the 1800s from Dora and the Irish-style ending -een and spread by Edna Lyall's 1894 novel Doreen. Dora shortens Dorothy and Theodora, built on Greek doron, gift.
A spelling of Barbara, from Greek barbaros, foreign. Saint Barbara made the name popular across Christian Europe; Barbra Streisand made this spelling famous by dropping an a.
A spelling of Catherine, from Greek Aikaterine; the traditional meaning pure comes from a later link with Greek katharos. Cathrine is also the usual Norwegian and Danish spelling.
A spelling of Cindy, the short form of Cynthia, a Greek title of the moon goddess Artemis, who was born on Mount Kynthos. Cindy has also served as a short form of Lucinda.
Of uncertain origin. It may be a form of Valda, built on the Germanic element wald, 'rule'; in the US it was used mostly in the early 1900s alongside Velma and Zelda.
An American name of the 1960s and 70s, a variant of Shanda and Shawnda, which add a -da ending to Shawn, the Irish form of John.
namesakes: Shonda Rhimes (creator of Grey's Anatomy and Scandal)
e.note: Sounds like the Yiddish word shande, often written shonda, meaning a shame or disgrace.

e.etymology: An elaboration of Rena or Renee with the -ita ending. Those names go back to Latin Renatus, 'born again', an early Christian name.
A respelling of Pamela, which the poet Sir Philip Sidney coined for his romance Arcadia around 1580, probably from Greek pan, 'all', and meli, 'honey'.
A spelling of Peggy, a medieval English pet form of Margaret that grew out of Meg and Meggy. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, 'pearl'.
A pet form of Henrietta, the feminine of Henry, from Germanic heim, 'home', and ric, 'ruler'. It was also used for Hester and Esther.
A respelling of Sharon, the Hebrew name of the fertile coastal plain of Israel, praised in the Song of Songs for its flowers. Sharon became a girls' name in the 20th century.
An American name of the 1960s that blends Tammy or Tamara with the ending of Pamela.
A spelling of Lou, the short form of Louise, Louisa and Lucinda for girls and of Louis for boys. Louis and Louise come from the Germanic name Chlodovech, 'famous in battle'.
First recorded in the US after George Barr McCutcheon's 1905 bestseller Nedra, where it is the name of an island. McCutcheon appears to have made it up.
A spelling of Tonya, a Russian pet form of Antonina that also serves as a short form of Antonia. Both come from the Roman family name Antonius, whose meaning is unknown.
A spelling of Shelly or Shelley, an English surname from places named with Old English scylf, 'ledge', and leah, 'clearing'. It is also a short form of Michelle and Rachel.
A pet form of Florence, from Latin florens, 'flourishing'; Florence Dombey is called Floy in Dickens's Dombey and Son. Around 1900 it was also given to American boys, close to Floyd.
A misspelling of Juanita that became a name of its own in US records. Juanita is the Spanish pet form of Juana, the feminine of Juan (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
A shortened American form of Dorothea, from Greek doron, 'gift', and theos, 'god'. It was most used in the 1910s and 20s, when Dorothy was at its height.
A spelling of Vern, the short form of Vernon, a Norman surname from a place named with Gaulish vern, 'alder'. The French surname Verne has the same root.
namesakes: Verne Troyer (actor, Mini-Me in Austin Powers)

assoc.t: Jules Verne, 19th-century French science fiction author

e.etymology: A pet form of Vernon for boys and of Verna or Laverne for girls. Vernon is a Norman surname from a place named with Gaulish vern, 'alder'.
A pet form of Claude or Claudia, from the Roman family name Claudius, traditionally derived from Latin claudus, 'lame'. In the US around 1900 it was given to both boys and girls.

assoc.t: Claudie Wells, American Girl's 1920s Harlem doll

e.etymology: A spelling of Carol, which began as a form of Charles (Latin Carolus, from Germanic karl, 'free man') and later served as a short form of Caroline. Caryl has been used for both sexes.
